In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of numerical schemes for the simulation of the Green Nagdi model for the propagation of fully nonlinear and dispersive surface water waves.
the development of numerical methods for solving the fully nonlinear shallow water equations.

the development of a new generation of numerical models for free surface wave propagation, which are able to capture the main nonlinear wave physics in a robust and accurate way, with a particular focus on breaking and run up phenomena.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the hybrid approach proposed in this paper is a very promising strategy for the simulation of wave propagation in the near shore regions, in particular in presence of breaking, run up and wave run down.

the fully coupled schemes are very accurate in reproducing wave dispersion, with a dispersion error of the same order of the standard fourth order finite difference scheme, and that they are also able to capture breaking, with a good qualitative and quantitative description of the wave evolution.

the hybrid approach, in its different versions, is able to reproduce with high accuracy the wave physics of the fully nonlinear and weak dispersion equations, and to provide an efficient and robust numerical tool for the simulation of near shore wave dynamics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are developing a new generation of wave models that are more efficient than traditional ones, while retaining the accuracy and the physics that are required for coastal applications.

we have developed a novel approach for the simulation of nonlinear wave propagation, wave breaking and run up that is based on the Green-Naghdi equations, a system of fully nonlinear shallow water equations that includes dispersive effects and that can capture wave breaking.

the proposed hybrid approach allows to recover energy dissipated during the wave breaking and run up processes, without the use of any ad hoc artificial dissipation term, while preserving the accuracy and efficiency of the fully nonlinear solution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the hybrid approach is a promising strategy for the simulation of wave breaking and run up.
the hybrid approach can be a valid strategy to recover wave dissipation and run up, with a computational cost comparable to the standard fully nonlinear model.

the hybrid approach is a very promising tool for the solution of nonlinear wave propagation, and that a careful analysis of the dispersion properties of the coupled schemes is crucial for a reliable implementation of such strategies.
